cards.explanation: The answer is that Job is claiming, "I am more righteous than God." Elihu asks, "Do you think this is just? You say, ‘I am more righteous than God.’" (Job 35:2) Those are Elihu's words about Job, and he puts them right on the table. I think that's a pretty heavy thing to say to a man who's hurting.

The question underneath is whether doing right even pays off. Elihu quotes Job asking, "What does it profit me, and what benefit do I gain apart from sin?" (Job 35:3) Profit and benefit are money words, so that's what Elihu hears in it. And he's about to answer.

The word is friends. Elihu says, "I will reply to you and to your friends as well." (Job 35:4) So Job isn't the only one getting an answer, because his friends are in it too. That's a full kitchen, friends, and everybody's getting a cookie.

Elihu's point is that sin can't harm God. He says, "If you sin, what do you accomplish against Him? If you multiply your transgressions, what do you do to Him?" (Job 35:6) He points Job at the clouds high above him, and then says sin doesn't touch God. I think the sky is there to show how high up God is.

The word is man. Elihu says, "Your wickedness affects only a man like yourself, and your righteousness only a son of man." (Job 35:8) He's saying it lands on people, not on God. Same goes for the good stuff, because a person is the one who feels it.

The question is "Where is God my Maker." Elihu says no one asks, "Where is God my Maker, who gives us songs in the night…" (Job 35:10) So in his telling, people cry out about the oppression but skip asking about God. That's how Elihu puts it, and I'll let his words stand.

The answer is True. Elihu says, "There they cry out, but He does not answer, because of the pride of evil men." (Job 35:12) That's what he says, and he gives a reason in the same breath. Remember, friends, these are Elihu's words, and he's talking about people crying out under oppression.

The reason Elihu gives is the pride of evil men. He says, "There they cry out, but He does not answer, because of the pride of evil men." (Job 35:12) Notice who the pride belongs to: evil men, not the ones crying out. That's Elihu's claim about why the cries go unanswered, and I'd keep it right there in his words.

The two words are listen and empty. Elihu says, "Surely God does not listen to empty pleas, and the Almighty does not take note of it." (Job 35:13) Just before it, he says that no one asks, "Where is God my Maker…" (Job 35:10), and that God does not answer "…because of the pride of evil men." (Job 35:12) I think that's what he means by empty pleas: cries that never look to God and come from pride. Then he turns to Job, "How much less, then, when you say that you do not see Him…" (Job 35:14), so Elihu is putting Job's complaint in the same camp.

The answer is False. Elihu says, "How much less, then, when you say that you do not see Him, that your case is before Him and you must wait for Him…" (Job 35:14) He's building on the empty pleas of verse 13. His point is that Job's words about not seeing God get even less of God's attention, not more.

The word is knowledge. Elihu finishes with, "So Job opens his mouth in vain and multiplies words without knowledge." (Job 35:16) That's the last thing he says in this passage. I think it's a hard thing to hear when you're already hurting (Job 2:7).
